/v1/projects/{ref}/config/realtime`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/realtime-config/patch/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/config/realtime)\\\\n\\\\nYou can manage the configuration of all services using the Management API.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Development workflow\\\\n\\\\nSupabase is a *stateful* service: we store data. If anything breaks in production, you can't \\\\\\\"roll back\\\\\\\" to a point in time because doing so might cause your users to lose any data that their production environment received since the last checkpoint.\\\\n\\\\nBecause of this, it's important that you adopt a development workflow on behalf of your users:\\\\n\\\\n![Change flow](/docs/img/integrations/change-flow.png)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating a `DEV` branch\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`POST /v1/projects/{ref}/branches`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/environments/post/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/branches)\\\\n\\\\nAfter launching a project, it's important that all changes happen on a development branch. Branches can be treated like ephemeral servers: if anything goes wrong you can either revert the changes or destroy the branch and create a new one based off of production.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl 'https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/branches' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{\\\\n    \\\\\\\"branch_name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"DEV\\\\\\\",\\\\n    \\\\\\\"secrets\\\\\\\": {\\\\n      \\\\\\\"STRIPE_SECRET_KEY\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"sk_test_123...\\\\\\\"\\\\n      \\\\\\\"STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY\\\\\\\":\\\\\\\"pk_test_123...\\\\\\\"\\\\n    }\\\\n  }'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Make database changes\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`POST /v1/projects/{ref}/database/migrations`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/database/post/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/database/migrations)\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Contact us for access to migrations endpoint\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Only select customers have access to database migrations endpoint. Submit this [form](/solutions/ai-builders#talk-to-partnerships-team) to get access.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nFor this example we will create a todos table using the [`POST /v1/projects/{ref}/database/migrations`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/database/post/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/database/migrations) endpoint.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate table public.todos (\\\\n  id serial primary key,\\\\n  task text not null\\\\n);\\\\n\\\\nalter table public.todos\\\\nenable row level security;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis endpoint will automatically create a migration inside the `supabase_migrations` schema and run the migration. If the schema migration fails, the changes will be rolled back.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/database/migrations \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{\\\\n    \\\\\\\"query\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"create table public.todos (id serial primary key, task text not null); alter table public.todos enable row level security;\\\\\\\",\\\\n    \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"Create a todos table\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Create a restore point\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Contact us for access to restore points\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Only select customers have access to restore points. Submit this [form](/solutions/ai-builders#talk-to-partnerships-team) to get access.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nAfter every change you make to the database, it's a good idea to create a restore point. This will allow you to roll back the database if you decide to go in a different direction.\\\\n\\\\nBeware that only database changes are captured when creating a restore point.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/database/backups/restore-point \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{\\\\n    \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"abcdefg\\\\\\\"\\\\n  }'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Reverting changes\\\\n\\\\n![Revert](/docs/img/integrations/revert.png)\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Contact us for access to restore points\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Only select customers have access to restore points. Submit this [form](/solutions/ai-builders#talk-to-partnerships-team) to get access.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating restore points, you are able to revert back to any restore point that you want.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/database/backups/undo \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"abcdefg\\\\\\\"\\\\n}'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWhen you revert changes, you are undo-ing all database changes since the specified restore point, including:\\\\n\\\\n*   Schema changes\\\\n*   Any seed data that you inserted\\\\n*   Any test users who have signed up (and auth tokens for sign ins)\\\\n*   Pointers to files in Supabase Storage.\\\\n\\\\nIt will not affect:\\\\n\\\\n*   Configuration changes\\\\n*   Any secrets that have been added\\\\n*   Storage objects themselves\\\\n*   Any deployed Edge Functions\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Add seed data\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Do not use production data in branches!\\\\\\\">\\\\n  It's important that the data in development branches is NOT production data, especially for non-developers who don't understand the implications of working with data. Security and side-effects (e.g. emailing all production users) are two reasons why this is important.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nIt's common in `DEV` branches to \\\\\\\"seed\\\\\\\" data. This is basically test data for users. Let's insert the following seed to our new todos table:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ninsert into todos (task)\\\\nvalues\\\\n  ('Task 1'),\\\\n  ('Task 2'),\\\\n  ('Task 3');\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nYou can use the `POST /database/query` endpoint to add data:\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{branch_ref}/database/query \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data-binary @- <<EOF\\\\n{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"query\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"insert into todos (task) values ('Task 1'), ('Task 2'), ('Task 3');\\\\\\\"\\\\n}\\\\nEOF\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Deploying Edge Functions\\\\n\\\\nYou can create and deploy Edge Functions on a branch and then merge them into Production.\\\\n\\\\n![Deploy Edge Functions](/docs/img/integrations/change-functions.png)\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/functions/deploy \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: multipart/form-data' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --form 'file=@path/to/function.zip' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --form 'metadata={\\\\n    \\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"my-function\\\\\\\",\\\\n    \\\\\\\"entrypoint_path\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"index.ts\\\\\\\",\\\\n    \\\\\\\"import_map_path\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"import_map.json\\\\\\\",\\\\n    \\\\\\\"static_patterns\\\\\\\": [\\\\\\\"assets/*\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"public/*\\\\\\\"],\\\\n    \\\\\\\"verify_jwt\\\\\\\": true\\\\n  }'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Merge all changes\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`POST /v1/branches/{branch_id_or_ref}/merge`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/environments/post/v1/branches/\\\\\\\\{branch_id_or_ref}/merge)\\\\n\\\\nOnce the changes have been made, you can merge the changes into the production project:\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/branches/{ref}/merge \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{}'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nMerging changes will automatically merge only the following:\\\\n\\\\n*   Database changes\\\\n*   Deployed Edge Functions\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Security checks for production\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`GET /v1/projects/{ref}/advisors/security`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/advisors/get/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/advisors/security)\\\\n\\\\nPrior to deploying to production we strongly recommend running the security advisor on the project to make sure the latest changes are secure.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/advisors/security \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request GET \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header  'Authorization: Bearer {PAT_OR_USER_TOKEN}' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Disaster recovery for production\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`POST /v1/projects/{ref}/database/backups/restore-pitr`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/database/post/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/database/backups/restore-pitr)\\\\n\\\\n![Rollback](/docs/img/integrations/rollback.png)\\\\n\\\\n*   Rollbacks can cause data loss. Only use it in `PROD` when absolutely necessary.\\\\n*   Only available in prod when a project has already explicitly enabled PITR prior to rolling back.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/database/backups/restore-pitr \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request POST \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer {PAT_OR_USER_TOKEN}' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data '{\\\\n  \\\\\\\"recovery_time_target_unix\\\\\\\": 1\\\\n}'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Claim flow\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`GET /v1/oauth/authorize/project-claim`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/oauth/get/v1/oauth/authorize/project-claim)\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Contact us for access to claim flow\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Only select customers have access to claim flow. Submit this [form](/solutions/ai-builders#talk-to-partnerships-team) to get access.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nYour users may want to claim the project that currently lives in your org so that they can have more control over it.\\\\n\\\\nWe've enabled transferring the project from your org to your user's org while you continue to retain access to interact with the project through an [OAuth integration](/docs/guides/integrations/build-a-supabase-oauth-integration).\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl -L \\\\\\\"https://api.supabase.com/v1/oauth/authorize/project-claim?project_ref={ref}&client_id={oauth_client_id}&response_type=code&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --request GET \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer {PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThe user is redirected to a Supabase UI:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Create a new Supabase account or sign in to an existing one\\\\n2.  Create a new Supabase Organization or select an existing one\\\\n3.  Review your OAuth integration's permission scopes\\\\n4.  Review the Project transfer details\\\\n5.  Confirm the OAuth integration and the Project transfer for the selected Organization\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Remove custom configuration before transferring project\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Before transferring the project to your user's org, make sure to remove any custom configuration that you do not want your user's project to retain.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Platform kit\\\\n\\\\nDocs: [https://supabase.com/ui/docs/platform/platform-kit](https://supabase.com/ui/docs/platform/platform-kit)\\\\n\\\\n<div className=\\\\\\\"video-container mb-8\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <iframe className=\\\\\\\"w-full\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"https://xguihxuzqibwxjnimxev.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/videos/marketing/blog/platform-kit/platform-kit.mp4\\\\\\\" title=\\\\\\\"Supabase UI: Platform Kit\\\\\\\" allow=\\\\\\\"accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; fullscreen; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share\\\\\\\" allowfullscreen autoplay muted loop playsInline />\\\\n</div>\\\\n\\\\nWe've created Platform Kit, a collection of UI components that interact with Management API, as a lightweight version of Supabase Dashboard that you can embed directly in your app so your users never have to leave in order to interact with the project.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Debugging projects\\\\n\\\\nManagement API endpoint: [`GET /v1/projects/{ref}/analytics/endpoints/logs.all`](https://api.supabase.com/api/v1#tag/analytics/get/v1/projects/\\\\\\\\{ref}/analytics/endpoints/logs.all)\\\\n\\\\nWhen you need to debug a project, you can query the project's logs to see if there are any errors and address them accordingly.\\\\n\\\\n```sh\\\\ncurl 'https://api.supabase.com/v1/projects/{ref}/analytics/endpoints/logs.all' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --get \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --header 'Authorization: Bearer YOUR_SECRET_TOKEN' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data-urlencode 'sql=SELECT datetime(timestamp), status_code, path, event_message\\\\n    FROM edge_logs\\\\n    CROSS JOIN UNNEST(metadata) AS metadata\\\\n    CROSS JOIN UNNEST(response) AS response\\\\n    WHERE status_code >= 400\\\\n    ORDER BY timestamp DESC\\\\n    LIMIT 100' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data-urlencode 'iso_timestamp_start=2025-03-23T00:00:00Z' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data-urlencode 'iso_timestamp_end=2025-03-23T01:00:00Z'\\\\n```\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Replication Setup\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-setup\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Replication Setup\\\\n\\\\nConfigure publications and destinations for replication.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"caution\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Private Alpha\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Replication is currently in private alpha. Access is limited and features may change.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\nReplication uses **Postgres logical replication** to stream changes from your database. Powered by [Supabase ETL](https://github.com/supabase/etl), an open source tool built for Postgres logical replication, it provides a managed interface through the Dashboard to configure and monitor replication pipelines.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Setup overview\\\\n\\\\nReplication requires two main components: a **Postgres publication** (defines what to replicate) and a **destination** (where data is sent). Follow these steps to set up your replication pipeline.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"tip\\\\\\\">\\\\n  If you already have a Postgres publication set up, you can skip to [Step 2: Enable replication](#step-2-enable-replication).\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Create a Postgres publication\\\\n\\\\nA Postgres publication defines which tables and change types will be replicated from your database. You create publications using SQL.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Creating a publication\\\\n\\\\nThe following SQL examples assume you have `users` and `orders` tables in your database.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for specific tables\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create publication for both tables\\\\ncreate publication pub_users_orders\\\\nfor table users, orders;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis publication will track all changes (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE) for both the `users` and `orders` tables.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for all tables in a schema\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a publication for all tables in the public schema\\\\ncreate publication pub_all_public for tables in schema public;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will track changes for all existing and future tables in the `public` schema.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Publication for all tables\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a publication for all tables\\\\ncreate publication pub_all_tables for all tables;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will track changes for all tables in your database.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Advanced publication options\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Selecting specific columns\\\\n\\\\nYou can replicate only a subset of columns from a table:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Replicate only specific columns from the users table\\\\ncreate publication pub_users_subset\\\\nfor table users (id, email, created_at);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nThis will only replicate the `id`, `email`, and `created_at` columns from the `users` table.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n##### Filtering rows with a predicate\\\\n\\\\nYou can filter which rows to replicate using a WHERE clause:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Only replicate active users\\\\ncreate publication pub_active_users\\\\nfor table users where (status = 'active');\\\\n\\\\n-- Only replicate recent orders\\\\ncreate publication pub_recent_orders\\\\nfor table orders where (created_at > '2024-01-01');\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Viewing publications in the Dashboard\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating a publication via SQL, you can view it in the Supabase Dashboard:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Navigate to **Database** \\u2192 [Publications](/dashboard/project/_/database/publications) in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n2.  You'll see all your publications listed with their tables\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Enable replication\\\\n\\\\nBefore adding destinations, you need to enable replication for your project:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Navigate to the [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) section in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n2.  Select the **replication** tab\\\\n3.  Click **Enable replication** to activate replication for your project\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Enable Replication\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-enable-replication.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3: Add a destination\\\\n\\\\nOnce replication is enabled and you have a Postgres publication, you can add a destination. The destination is where your replicated data will be stored, while the pipeline is the active Postgres replication process that continuously streams changes from your database to that destination.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Choose and configure your destination\\\\n\\\\nFollow these steps to configure your destination. The specific configuration depends on which destination type you choose. Both Analytics Buckets and BigQuery destinations are supported, though availability varies based on the planned roll-out strategy.\\\\n\\\\n<Tabs scrollable size=\\\\\\\"small\\\\\\\" type=\\\\\\\"underlined\\\\\\\" defaultActiveId=\\\\\\\"analytics-buckets\\\\\\\" queryGroup=\\\\\\\"destination\\\\\\\">\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"analytics-buckets\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Analytics Buckets\\\\\\\">\\\\n    [Analytics Buckets](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/introduction) are specialized storage buckets in Supabase Storage designed for analytical workloads. They provide S3-compatible storage and use the [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/) open table format, making your data accessible via standard tools like DuckDB, Spark, and other analytics platforms.\\\\n\\\\n    When you replicate to Analytics Buckets, your database changes are automatically written in Iceberg format, creating tables in object storage that you can query for analytics.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 1: Create an analytics bucket\\\\n\\\\n    First, create an analytics bucket to store your replicated data:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Storage](/dashboard/project/_/storage/buckets) \\u2192 **Analytics** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **New bucket**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Create new analytics bucket\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-iceberg-new-bucket.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Fill in the bucket details:\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Analytics bucket details\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-iceberg-details.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Name**: A unique name for your bucket (e.g., `analytics_warehouse`)\\\\n        *   **Region**: Select the region where your data will be stored\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Click **Create bucket**\\\\n\\\\n    5.  **Copy the credentials** displayed after bucket creation. You'll need these in the next steps:\\\\n        *   **Catalog Token**: Authentication token for accessing the Iceberg catalog\\\\n        *   **S3 Access Key ID**: Access key for S3-compatible storage\\\\n        *   **S3 Secret Access Key**: Secret key for S3-compatible storage\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 2: Configure analytics buckets as a destination\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) \\u2192 **replication** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **Add destination**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"Add Destination\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-add-destination.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Configure the general settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Destination name**: A name to identify this destination (e.g., \\\\\\\"Analytics Warehouse\\\\\\\")\\\\n        *   **Publication**: The publication to replicate data from (created in [Step 1](#step-1-create-a-postgres-publication))\\\\n        *   **Destination type**: Select **Analytics Buckets**\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Configure Analytics Buckets settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Bucket**: The name of your analytics bucket from Step 1\\\\n        *   **Namespace**: The schema name where your tables will be replicated (e.g., `public`)\\\\n        *   **Catalog Token**: Authentication token from Step 1\\\\n        *   **S3 Access Key ID**: Access key from Step 1\\\\n        *   **S3 Secret Access Key**: Secret key from Step 1\\\\n\\\\n    5.  Configure **Advanced Settings** (optional):\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Batch wait time (milliseconds)**: How long to wait for more changes before sending a batch. Default is recommended for optimal performance.\\\\n\\\\n    6.  Click **Create and start** to begin replication\\\\n\\\\n    Your replication pipeline will now start copying data from your database to the analytics bucket in Iceberg format.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How it works\\\\n\\\\n    Once configured, replication to Analytics Buckets:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Captures changes from your Postgres database (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE operations)\\\\n    2.  Batches changes for optimal performance\\\\n    3.  Creates Iceberg tables automatically to match your Postgres schema\\\\n    4.  Streams data to Analytics Buckets\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How tables are structured\\\\n\\\\n    Replicated tables use a changelog structure:\\\\n\\\\n    *   Tables are created with a `_changelog` suffix in the name (e.g., `users_changelog`)\\\\n    *   Each table contains a `cdc_operation` column indicating the operation type: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, or `TRUNCATE`\\\\n    *   This append-only format preserves the complete history of all changes\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Limitations\\\\n\\\\n    *   **Append-only log**: Currently provides an append-only log format rather than a full table representation\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Additional resources\\\\n\\\\n    *   [Analytics Buckets documentation](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/introduction) - Learn more about Analytics Buckets and S3-compatible storage\\\\n    *   [Realtime Data Sync to Analytics Buckets](/docs/guides/storage/analytics/replication) - Step-by-step guide for replicating to Analytics Buckets\\\\n    *   [Apache Iceberg](https://iceberg.apache.org/) - Official Iceberg documentation\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n\\\\n  <TabPanel id=\\\\\\\"bigquery\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"BigQuery\\\\\\\">\\\\n    [BigQuery](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery) is Google's fully managed data warehouse. You can replicate your database tables to BigQuery for analytics and reporting.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 1: Prepare GCP resources\\\\n\\\\n    Before configuring BigQuery as a destination, set up the following in Google Cloud Platform:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  **Google Cloud Platform (GCP) account**: [Sign up for GCP](https://cloud.google.com/gcp) if you don't have one\\\\n\\\\n    2.  **BigQuery dataset**: Create a [BigQuery dataset](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/datasets-intro) in your GCP project\\\\n\\\\n        *   Open the BigQuery console in GCP\\\\n        *   Select your project\\\\n        *   Click \\\\\\\"Create Dataset\\\\\\\"\\\\n        *   Provide a dataset ID (e.g., `supabase_replication`)\\\\n\\\\n    3.  **GCP service account key**: Create a [service account](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/keys-create-delete) with appropriate permissions:\\\\n\\\\n        *   Go to IAM & Admin \\u2192 Service Accounts\\\\n        *   Click \\\\\\\"Create Service Account\\\\\\\"\\\\n        *   Grant the **BigQuery Data Editor** role\\\\n        *   Create and download the JSON key file\\\\n\\\\n        Required permissions:\\\\n\\\\n        *   `bigquery.datasets.get`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.create`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.get`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.getData`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.update`\\\\n        *   `bigquery.tables.updateData`\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Step 2: Configure BigQuery as a destination\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Navigate to [Database](/dashboard/project/_/database/replication) \\u2192 **replication** in your Supabase Dashboard\\\\n\\\\n    2.  Click **Add destination**\\\\n\\\\n            <Image alt=\\\\\\\"BigQuery Configuration Settings\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-bigquery-details.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n    3.  Configure the general settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Destination name**: A name to identify this destination (e.g., \\\\\\\"BigQuery Warehouse\\\\\\\")\\\\n        *   **Publication**: The publication to replicate data from (created in [Step 1](#step-1-create-a-postgres-publication))\\\\n        *   **Destination type**: Select **BigQuery**\\\\n\\\\n    4.  Configure BigQuery-specific settings:\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Project ID**: Your BigQuery project identifier (found in the GCP Console)\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Dataset ID**: The name of your BigQuery dataset (without the project ID)\\\\n\\\\n                <Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n                  In the GCP Console, the dataset is shown as `project-id.dataset-id`. Enter only the part after the dot. For example, if you see `my-project.my_dataset`, enter `my_dataset`.\\\\n                </Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Service Account Key**: Your GCP service account key in JSON format (from Step 1)\\\\n\\\\n    5.  Configure **Advanced Settings** (optional):\\\\n\\\\n        *   **Batch wait time (milliseconds)**: How long to wait for more changes before sending a batch. Default is recommended for optimal performance.\\\\n\\\\n    6.  Click **Create and start** to begin replication\\\\n\\\\n    Your replication pipeline will now start copying data from your database to BigQuery.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How it works\\\\n\\\\n    Once configured, replication to BigQuery:\\\\n\\\\n    1.  Captures changes from your Postgres database (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE operations)\\\\n    2.  Batches changes for optimal performance\\\\n    3.  Creates BigQuery tables automatically to match your Postgres schema\\\\n    4.  Streams data to BigQuery\\\\n\\\\n    ##### How tables are structured\\\\n\\\\n    Due to BigQuery limitations, replicated tables use a versioned structure:\\\\n\\\\n    *   The table you query is a **view** (e.g., `users`)\\\\n    *   The actual data is stored in versioned tables with a `_version` suffix (e.g., `users_version`)\\\\n    *   When a table is truncated in your database, a new version is created and the view automatically points to the latest version\\\\n\\\\n    This structure handles table truncations seamlessly while maintaining query compatibility.\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Limitations\\\\n\\\\n    *   **Row size**: Limited to 10 MB per row due to BigQuery Storage Write API constraints\\\\n\\\\n    ##### Additional resources\\\\n\\\\n    *   [BigQuery documentation](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs) - Official Google BigQuery documentation\\\\n  </TabPanel>\\\\n</Tabs>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4: Monitor your pipeline\\\\n\\\\nAfter creating a destination, the replication pipeline will start and appear in the destinations list. You can monitor the pipeline's status and performance from the Dashboard.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Replication Destinations List\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-destinations-list.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\nFor comprehensive monitoring instructions including pipeline states, metrics, and logs, see the [Replication Monitoring guide](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-monitoring).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Managing your pipeline\\\\n\\\\nYou can manage your pipeline from the destinations list using the actions menu.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"Pipeline Actions\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/replication/replication-pipeline-actions.png\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\nAvailable actions:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Start**: Begin replication for a stopped pipeline\\\\n*   **Stop**: Pause replication (changes will queue up in the WAL)\\\\n*   **Restart**: Stop and start the pipeline (required after publication changes)\\\\n*   **Edit destination**: Modify destination settings like credentials or advanced options\\\\n*   **Delete**: Remove the destination and permanently stop replication\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Adding or removing tables\\\\n\\\\nIf you need to modify which tables are replicated after your replication pipeline is already running, follow these steps:\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  If your Postgres publication uses `FOR ALL TABLES` or `FOR TABLES IN SCHEMA`, new tables in that scope are automatically included in the publication. However, you still **must restart the replication pipeline** for the changes to take effect.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Adding tables to replication\\\\n\\\\n1.  Add the table to your publication using SQL:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    -- Add a single table to an existing publication\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders add table products;\\\\n\\\\n    -- Or add multiple tables at once\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders add table products, categories;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n2.  **Restart the replication pipeline** using the actions menu (see [Managing your pipeline](#managing-your-pipeline)) for the changes to take effect.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Removing tables from replication\\\\n\\\\n1.  Remove the table from your Postgres publication using SQL:\\\\n\\\\n    ```sql\\\\n    -- Remove a single table from a publication\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders drop table orders;\\\\n\\\\n    -- Or remove multiple tables at once\\\\n    alter publication pub_users_orders drop table orders, products;\\\\n    ```\\\\n\\\\n2.  **Restart the replication pipeline** using the actions menu (see [Managing your pipeline](#managing-your-pipeline)) for the changes to take effect.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Deleted tables are automatically recreated by the pipeline. To permanently delete a table, pause the pipeline first or remove it from the publication before deleting. See the [FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq#what-happens-if-a-table-is-deleted-at-the-destination) for details.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### How it works\\\\n\\\\nOnce configured, replication:\\\\n\\\\n1.  **Captures** changes from your Postgres database using Postgres publications and logical replication\\\\n2.  **Streams** the changes through the replication pipeline\\\\n3.  **Loads** the data to your destination in near real-time batches\\\\n\\\\nChanges are sent in batches to optimize performance and reduce costs. The batch size and timing can be adjusted using the advanced settings. The replication pipeline currently performs data extraction and loading only, without transformation - your data is replicated as-is to the destination.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Troubleshooting\\\\n\\\\nIf you encounter issues during setup:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Publication not appearing**: Ensure you created the Postgres publication via SQL and refresh the dashboard\\\\n*   **Tables not showing in publication**: Verify your tables have primary keys (required for Postgres logical replication)\\\\n*   **Pipeline failed to start**: Check the error message in the status view for specific details\\\\n*   **No data being replicated**: Verify your Postgres publication includes the correct tables and event types\\\\n\\\\nFor more troubleshooting help, see the [Replication FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Limitations\\\\n\\\\nReplication has the following limitations:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Primary keys required**: Tables must have primary keys (Postgres logical replication requirement)\\\\n*   **Custom data types**: Not supported\\\\n*   **Schema changes**: Not automatically handled\\\\n*   **No data transformation**: Data is replicated as-is without transformation\\\\n*   **Data duplicates**: Duplicates can occur when stopping a pipeline if your database has transactions that take longer than a few minutes to complete. See [Can data duplicates occur?](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq#can-data-duplicates-occur-during-pipeline-operations) for details\\\\n\\\\nDestination-specific limitations (such as Iceberg's append-only log format or BigQuery's row size limits) are detailed in each destination tab in [Step 3](#step-3-add-a-destination) above.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Future work\\\\n\\\\nReplication is actively being developed. Planned improvements include:\\\\n\\\\n*   **DDL support**: Automatic handling of Postgres schema changes (ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, etc.)\\\\n*   **Additional destinations**: Support for more data warehouses and analytics platforms\\\\n\\\\nThere are no public timelines for these features, but they represent the roadmap for making replication more robust and flexible.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Next steps\\\\n\\\\n*   [Monitor Replication](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-monitoring)\\\\n*   [View Replication FAQ](/docs/guides/database/replication/replication-faq)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"OrioleDB Overview\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/orioledb\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# OrioleDB Overview\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nThe [OrioleDB](https://www.orioledb.com/) Postgres extension provides a drop-in replacement storage engine for the default heap storage method. It is designed to improve Postgres' scalability and performance.\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB addresses PostgreSQL's scalability limitations by removing bottlenecks in the shared memory cache under high concurrency. It also optimizes write-ahead-log (WAL) insertion through row-level WAL logging. These changes lead to significant improvements in the industry standard TPC-C benchmark, which approximates a real-world transactional workload. The following benchmark was performed on a c7g.metal instance and shows OrioleDB's performance outperforming the default Postgres heap method with a 3.3x speedup.\\\\n\\\\n<Image alt=\\\\\\\"TPC-C (warehouses = 500)\\\\\\\" src=\\\\\\\"/docs/img/database/orioledb-tpc-c-500-warehouse.png\\\\\\\" className=\\\\\\\"max-w-[550px] !mx-auto border rounded-md\\\\\\\" zoomable />\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  OrioleDB is in active development and currently has [certain limitations](https://www.orioledb.com/docs/usage/getting-started#current-limitations). Currently, only B-tree indexes are supported, so features like pg\\\\\\\\_vector's HNSW indexes are not yet available. An Index Access Method bridge to unlock support for all index types used with heap storage is under active development. In the Supabase OrioleDB image the default storage method has been updated to use OrioleDB, granting better performance out of the box.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Concepts\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Index-organized tables\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB uses index-organized tables, where table data is stored in the index structure. This design eliminates the need for separate heap storage, reduces overhead and improves lookup performance for primary key queries.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### No buffer mapping\\\\n\\\\nIn-memory pages are connected to the storage pages using direct links. This allows OrioleDB to bypass PostgreSQL's shared buffer pool and eliminate the associated complexity and contention in buffer mapping.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Undo log\\\\n\\\\nMulti-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) is implemented using an undo log. The undo log stores previous row versions and transaction information, which enables consistent reads while removing the need for table vacuuming completely.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Copy-on-write checkpoints\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB implements copy-on-write checkpoints to persist data efficiently. This approach writes only modified data during a checkpoint, reducing the I/O overhead compared to traditional Postgres checkpointing and allowing row-level WAL logging.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Usage\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating OrioleDB project\\\\n\\\\nYou can get started with OrioleDB by enabling the extension in your Supabase dashboard.\\\\nTo get started with OrioleDB you need to [create a new Supabase project](/dashboard/new/_) and choose `OrioleDB Public Alpha` Postgres version.\\\\n\\\\n<Image\\\\n  alt=\\\\\\\"Creating OrioleDB project\\\\\\\"\\\\n  src={{\\\\n    light: '/docs/img/database/orioledb-creating-project--light.png',\\\\n    dark: '/docs/img/database/orioledb-creating-project.png',\\\\n  }}\\\\n  className=\\\\\\\"max-w-[550px] !mx-auto border rounded-md\\\\\\\"\\\\n  zoomable\\\\n/>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating tables\\\\n\\\\nTo create a table using the OrioleDB storage engine just execute the standard `CREATE TABLE` statement. By default it will create a table using OrioleDB storage engine. For example:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create a table\\\\ncreate table blog_post (\\\\n  id int8 not null,\\\\n  title text not null,\\\\n  body text not null,\\\\n  author text not null,\\\\n  published_at timestamptz not null default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,\\\\n  views bigint not null,\\\\n  primary key (id)\\\\n);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Creating indexes\\\\n\\\\nOrioleDB tables always have a primary key. If it wasn't defined explicitly, a hidden primary key is created using the `ctid` column.\\\\nAdditionally you can create secondary indexes.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Currently, only B-tree indexes are supported, so features like pg\\\\\\\\_vector's HNSW indexes are not yet available.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create an index\\\\ncreate index blog_post_published_at on blog_post (published_at);\\\\n\\\\ncreate index blog_post_views on blog_post (views) where (views > 1000);\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Data manipulation\\\\n\\\\nYou can query and modify data in OrioleDB tables using standard SQL statements, including `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` and `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`.\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nINSERT INTO blog_post (id, title, body, author, views)\\\\nVALUES (1, 'Hello, World!', 'This is my first blog post.', 'John Doe', 1000);\\\\n\\\\nSELECT * FROM Supabase\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/platform/migrating-to-supabase/postgres\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Migrate from Postgres to Supabase\\\\n\\\\nMigrate your existing Postgres database to Supabase.\\\\n\\\\nThis is a guide for migrating your Postgres database to [Supabase](https://supabase.com).\\\\nSupabase is a robust and open-source platform. Supabase provides all the backend features developers need to build a product: a Postgres database, authentication, instant APIs, edge functions, real-time subscriptions, and storage. Postgres is the core of Supabase\\u2014for example, you can use row-level security, and there are more than 40 Postgres extensions available.\\\\n\\\\nThis guide demonstrates how to migrate your Postgres database to Supabase to get the most out of Postgres while gaining access to all the features you need to build a project.\\\\n\\\\nThis guide provides three methods for migrating your Postgres database to Supabase:\\\\n\\\\n1.  **Google Colab** - Guided notebook with copy-paste workflow\\\\n2.  **Manual Dump/Restore** - CLI approach, works for all versions\\\\n3.  **Logical Replication** - Minimal downtime, requires Postgres 10+\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Connection modes\\\\n\\\\nSupabase provides the following connection modes:\\\\n\\\\n*   Direct connection\\\\n*   Supavisor session mode\\\\n*   Supavisor transaction mode\\\\n\\\\nUse Supavisor session mode for the database migration tasks (pg\\\\\\\\_dump/restore and logical replication).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Method 1: Google Colab (easiest)\\\\n\\\\nSupabase provides a Google Colab migration notebook for a guided migration experience:\\\\n[Supabase Migration Colab Notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/mansueli/Supa-Migrate/blob/main/Migrate_Postgres_Supabase.ipynb)\\\\n\\\\nThis is ideal if you prefer a step-by-step, copy-paste workflow with minimal setup.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Method 2: Manual dump/restore\\\\n\\\\nThis method works for all Postgres versions using CLI tools.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Prerequisites\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Source Postgres requirements\\\\n\\\\n*   Connection string with rights to run `pg_dump`\\\\n*   No special settings required for dump/restore\\\\n*   Network access from migration VM\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Migration environment\\\\n\\\\n*   Cloud VM running Ubuntu in the same region as source or target database\\\\n*   Postgres client tools matching your source database version\\\\n*   tmux for session persistence\\\\n*   Sufficient disk space (usually ~50% of source database size is enough, but varies case by case)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Pre-Migration checklist\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Check database size\\\\nselect pg_size_pretty(pg_database_size(current_database())) as size;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check Postgres version\\\\nselect version();\\\\n\\\\n-- List installed extensions\\\\nselect * from pg_extension order by extname;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check active connections\\\\nselect count(*) from pg_stat_activity;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Check available extensions in Supabase\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Connect to your Supabase database and check available extensions\\\\nSELECT name, comment FROM pg_available_extensions ORDER BY name;\\\\n\\\\n-- Compare with source database extensions\\\\nSELECT extname FROM pg_extension ORDER BY extname;\\\\n\\\\n-- Install needed extensions\\\\nCREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS extension_name;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Set up migration VM\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"tip\\\\\\\">\\\\n  For optimal performance, run the migration from a cloud VM, not your local machine. The VM should be in the same region as either your source or target database to optimize network performance. See the Resource Requirements table in Step 2 for VM sizing recommendations.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Set up Ubuntu VM\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Install Postgres client and tools\\\\nsudo apt update\\\\nsudo apt install software-properties-common\\\\nsudo sh -c 'echo \\\\\\\"deb http://apt.Postgres.org/pub/repos/apt $(lsb_release -cs)-pgdg main\\\\\\\" > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/pgdg.list'\\\\nwget --quiet -O - https://www.Postgres.org/media/keys/ACCC4CF8.asc | sudo apt-key add -\\\\nsudo apt update\\\\nsudo apt install Postgres-client-17 tmux htop iotop moreutils\\\\n\\\\n# Start or attach to tmux session\\\\ntmux a -t migration || tmux new -s migration\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Prepare Supabase project\\\\n\\\\n1.  Create a Supabase project at [supabase.com/dashboard](/dashboard)\\\\n2.  Note your database password\\\\n3.  Install required extensions via SQL or Dashboard\\\\n4.  Get your connection string:\\\\n    *   Go to **Project \\u2192 Settings \\u2192 Database \\u2192 Connection Pooling**\\\\n    *   Select **Session pooler** (port 5432) and copy the connection string\\\\n    *   Connection format: `Postgres://postgres.[ref]:[password]@aws-0-[region].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres`\\\\n\\\\n**Important Notes**:\\\\n\\\\n*   **Users/roles are not migrated** - You'll need to recreate roles and privileges after import ([Supabase Roles Guide](/blog/postgres-roles-and-privileges))\\\\n*   **Row Level Security (RLS) status on tables is not migrated** - You'll need to enable RLS for tables after migration.\\\\n\\\\n**Resource Requirements**:\\\\n\\\\n| Database Size | Recommended Compute | Recommended VM            | Action Required                                 |\\\\n| ------------- | ------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |\\\\n| \\\\\\\\< 10 GB      | Default             | 2 vCPUs, 4 GB RAM         | None                                            |\\\\n| 10-100 GB     | Default-Small       | 4 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM         | Consider compute upgrade                        |\\\\n| 100-500 GB    | Large compute       | 8 vCPUs, 16 GB RAM, NVMe  | Upgrade compute before restore                  |\\\\n| 500 GB - 1 TB | XL compute          | 16 vCPUs, 32 GB RAM, NVMe | Upgrade compute before restore                  |\\\\n| > 1 TB        | Custom              | Custom                    | [Contact support](/dashboard/support/new) first |\\\\n\\\\nAlso, you can temporarily increase compute size and/or disk IOPS and throughput via Settings \\u2192 Compute and Disk if you want faster database restore (you can use larger -j for pg\\\\\\\\_restore if you do so).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3: Create database dump\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Set source database to read only mode for production migration\\\\n\\\\nIf doing a maintenance window migration, prevent data changes:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Connect to source database and run:\\\\nALTER DATABASE your_database_name SET default_transaction_read_only = true;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nFor testing without a maintenance window, skip this step but use lower -j values.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Dump the database\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Determine number of parallel jobs based on:\\\\n# - Source database CPU cores (don't saturate production)\\\\n# - VM CPU cores\\\\n# - For testing without maintenance window: use lower values to be gentle\\\\n# - For production with maintenance window: can use higher values\\\\n\\\\nDUMP_JOBS=4  # Adjust based on your setup\\\\n\\\\n# Check available cores on VM\\\\nnproc\\\\n\\\\n# Create dump with progress logging\\\\npg_dump \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --host=<source_host> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --port=<source_port> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --username=<source_username> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --dbname=<source_database> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --jobs=$DUMP_JOBS \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --format=directory \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-owner \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-privileges \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-subscriptions \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --verbose \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --file=./db_dump 2>&1 | ts | tee -a dump.log\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n**Notes about dump flags**:\\\\n\\\\n*   `--no-owner --no-privileges`: Applied at dump time to prevent Supabase user management conflicts. While these could be used in pg\\\\\\\\_restore instead, applying them during dump keeps the dump file cleaner and more portable.\\\\n*   `--no-subscriptions`: Logical replication subscriptions won't work in the target\\\\n*   The dump captures all data and schema but excludes ownership/privileges that would conflict with Supabase's managed environment\\\\n*   To only migrate a single database schema, add the `--schema=PATTERN` parameter to your `pg_dump` command.\\\\n*   To exclude a schema: `--exclude-schema=PATTERN`.\\\\n*   To only migrate a single table: `--table=PATTERN`.\\\\n*   To exclude a table: `--exclude-table=PATTERN`.\\\\n\\\\nRun `pg_dump --help` for a full list of options.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Recommended parallelization (-j values)\\\\n\\\\n| Database Size | Testing (no maintenance window) | Production (with maintenance window) | Limiting Factor |\\\\n| ------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | --------------- |\\\\n| \\\\\\\\< 10 GB      | 2                               | 4                                    | Source CPU      |\\\\n| 10-100 GB     | 2-4                             | 8                                    | Source CPU      |\\\\n| 100-500 GB    | 4                               | 16                                   | Disk IOPS       |\\\\n| 500 GB - 1 TB | 4-8                             | 16-32                                | Disk IOPS + CPU |\\\\n\\\\n**Note**: For testing without a maintenance window, use lower -j values to avoid impacting production performance.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4: Restore to Supabase\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Set connection and restore\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Set Supabase connection (Session Pooler on port 5432 or direct connection)\\\\nexport SUPABASE_DB_URL=\\\\\\\"Postgres://postgres.[ref]:[password]@aws-0-[region].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n# Determine restore parallelization based on your Supabase compute size:\\\\n# Free tier: 2 cores \\u2192 use -j 2\\\\n# Small compute: 2 cores \\u2192 use -j 2\\\\n# Medium compute: 4 cores \\u2192 use -j 4\\\\n# Large compute: 8 cores \\u2192 use -j 8\\\\n# XL compute: 16 cores \\u2192 use -j 16\\\\n\\\\nRESTORE_JOBS=8  # Adjust based on your Supabase compute size\\\\n\\\\n# Restore the dump (parallel mode)\\\\n# Note: -j cannot be used with --single-transaction\\\\npg_restore \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --dbname=\\\\\\\"$SUPABASE_DB_URL\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --jobs=$RESTORE_JOBS \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --format=directory \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-owner \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-privileges \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --verbose \\\\\\\\\\\\n  ./db_dump 2>&1 | ts | tee -a restore.log\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nIf restore fails with extension errors, check that errors are only extension-related.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 5: Post-Migration tasks\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Update statistics (important)\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\npsql \\\\\\\"$SUPABASE_DB_URL\\\\\\\" -c \\\\\\\"VACUUM VERBOSE ANALYZE;\\\\\\\"\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\">\\\\n  For Postgres 18+, pg\\\\\\\\_dump includes statistics with `--with-statistics`, but you should still run VACUUM for optimal performance.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Verify migration\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Check row counts\\\\nselect schemaname, tablename, n_live_tup\\\\nfrom pg_stat_user_tables\\\\norder by n_live_tup desc\\\\nlimit 20;\\\\n-- Verify data with application-specific queries\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Re-enable writes on source (if keeping it)\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nALTER DATABASE your_database_name SET default_transaction_read_only = false;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Migration time estimates\\\\n\\\\n| Database Size | Dump Time | Restore Time | Total Time  |\\\\n| ------------- | --------- | ------------ | ----------- |\\\\n| 10 GB         | ~5 min   | ~10 min     | ~15 min    |\\\\n| 100 GB        | ~30 min  | ~45 min     | ~1.5 hours |\\\\n| 500 GB        | ~2 hours | ~3 hours    | ~5 hours   |\\\\n| 1 TB          | ~4 hours | ~6 hours    | ~10 hours  |\\\\n\\\\n*Times vary based on hardware, network, and parallelization settings*\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Important notes\\\\n\\\\n1.  **Region proximity matters**: VM should be in the same region as the source or target for best performance\\\\n2.  **Downgrade migrations**: While technically possible in some cases, highly not recommended\\\\n3.  **Testing without downtime**: Use lower `-j` values for pg\\\\\\\\_dump to avoid impacting production\\\\n4.  **For pg\\\\\\\\_restore**: Can use full parallelization regardless of production impact\\\\n5.  **Monitor resources**: Watch CPU, disk I/O with `htop`, `iotop`\\\\n6.  **Disk I/O**: Often the bottleneck before network bandwidth\\\\n\\\\n***\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Method 3: Logical replication\\\\n\\\\nThis method allows migration with minimal downtime using Postgres's logical replication feature. Requires Postgres 10+ on both source and target.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### When to use logical replication\\\\n\\\\n*   You need minimal downtime (minutes instead of hours)\\\\n*   Source database is Postgres 10 or higher\\\\n*   You can configure logical replication on the source\\\\n*   Database has high write activity that can't be paused for long\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Source Postgres prerequisites\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Access & privileges\\\\n\\\\n*   Connection string with rights to CREATE PUBLICATION and read tables\\\\n*   Superuser or replication privileges recommended\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Required settings for logical replication\\\\n\\\\n*   `wal_level = logical`\\\\n*   `max_wal_senders \\u2265 1`\\\\n*   `max_replication_slots \\u2265 1`\\\\n*   Sufficient `max_connections` (current + 1 for subscription)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Replica identity\\\\n\\\\nEvery table receiving UPDATE/DELETE must have a replica identity (typically a PRIMARY KEY). For tables without one:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nALTER TABLE schema.table_name REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Non-Replicated items\\\\n\\\\n*   **DDL changes** (schema modifications)\\\\n*   **Sequences** (need manual sync)\\\\n*   **Large Objects (LOBs)** (use dump/restore or store in regular bytea columns)\\\\n\\\\nPlan a schema freeze, sequence sync before cutover, and handle LOBs separately.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 1: Configure source database\\\\n\\\\nEdit Postgres configuration files:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### Postgres.conf\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Set Supabase connection (Session Pooler on port 5432 or direct connection)\\\\nexport SUPABASE_DB_URL=\\\\\\\"Postgres://postgres.[ref]:[password]@aws-0-[region].pooler.supabase.com:5432/postgres\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n# Set WAL level to logical\\\\nwal_level = logical\\\\n\\\\n# Ensure sufficient replication slots\\\\nmax_replication_slots = 10\\\\n\\\\n# Ensure sufficient WAL senders\\\\nmax_wal_senders = 10\\\\n\\\\n# Set appropriate max_connections (current connections + 1 for subscription)\\\\nmax_connections = 200  # Adjust based on your needs\\\\n\\\\n# Optional: Enable SSL for secure replication\\\\nssl = on\\\\n\\\\n# Allow connections from Supabase\\\\nlisten_addresses = '*'  # Or specific IP addresses\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n{/* supa-mdx-lint-disable-next-line Rule001HeadingCase */}\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n#### pg\\\\\\\\_hba.conf\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Allow replication connections from Supabase\\\\n# Replace <supabase_ip_range> with actual Supabase IP range\\\\nhost    replication     all     <supabase_ip_range>    md5\\\\nhost    all            all     <supabase_ip_range>    md5\\\\n\\\\n# With SSL:\\\\nhostssl replication     all     <supabase_ip_range>    md5\\\\nhostssl all            all     <supabase_ip_range>    md5\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nRestart Postgres:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\nsudo systemctl restart Postgres\\\\nsudo systemctl status Postgres\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 2: Verify configuration\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Should return 'logical'\\\\nSHOW wal_level;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check other parameters\\\\nSHOW max_replication_slots;\\\\nSHOW max_wal_senders;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check current connections\\\\nSELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 3: Check and set replica identity\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Find tables without primary keys\\\\nSELECT n.nspname, c.relname\\\\nFROM pg_class c\\\\nJOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace\\\\nLEFT JOIN pg_constraint pk ON pk.conrelid = c.oid AND pk.contype = 'p'\\\\nWHERE c.relkind = 'r'\\\\n  AND pk.oid IS NULL\\\\n  AND n.nspname NOT IN ('pg_catalog','information_schema');\\\\n\\\\n-- For tables without a primary key, set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL\\\\nALTER TABLE my_schema.my_table REPLICA IDENTITY FULL;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 4: Export and restore schema only\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Export schema from source\\\\npg_dump \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -h <source_host> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -U <source_user> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -p <source_port> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -d <source_database> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --schema-only \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-privileges \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-subscriptions \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --format=directory \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -f ./schema_dump\\\\n\\\\n# Restore schema to Supabase (use Session Pooler)\\\\npg_restore \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --dbname=\\\\\\\"$SUPABASE_DB_URL\\\\\\\" \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --format=directory \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --schema-only \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --no-privileges \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --single-transaction \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --verbose \\\\\\\\\\\\n  ./schema_dump\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 5: Create publication on source\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create publication for all tables\\\\nCREATE PUBLICATION supabase_migration FOR ALL TABLES;\\\\n\\\\n-- Or for specific tables only (doesn't require superuser)\\\\nCREATE PUBLICATION supabase_migration FOR TABLE\\\\n  schema1.table1,\\\\n  schema1.table2,\\\\n  public.table3;\\\\n\\\\n-- Verify publication was created\\\\nSELECT * FROM pg_publication;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 6: Create subscription on Supabase\\\\n\\\\nConnect to your Supabase database:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Create subscription with SSL (recommended)\\\\nCREATE SUBSCRIPTION supabase_subscription\\\\nCONNECTION 'host=<source_host> port=<source_port> user=<source_user> password=<source_password> dbname=<source_database> sslmode=require'\\\\nPUBLICATION supabase_migration;\\\\n\\\\n-- Or without SSL (if source doesn't support it)\\\\nCREATE SUBSCRIPTION supabase_subscription\\\\nCONNECTION 'host=<source_host> port=<source_port> user=<source_user> password=<source_password> dbname=<source_database> sslmode=disable'\\\\nPUBLICATION supabase_migration;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 7: Monitor replication status\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- On Supabase (subscriber) - check subscription status\\\\nselect * from pg_subscription_rel;\\\\n\\\\n-- srsubstate = 'r' means ready (synchronized)\\\\n-- srsubstate = 'i' means initializing\\\\n-- srsubstate = 'd' means data is being copied\\\\n\\\\n-- Overall subscription status\\\\nselect * from pg_stat_subscription;\\\\n\\\\n-- On source database - check replication status\\\\nselect * from pg_stat_replication;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check replication lag\\\\nselect\\\\n  slot_name,\\\\n  pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) as lag_size\\\\nfrom pg_replication_slots;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\nWait until all tables show `srsubstate = 'r'` (ready) status.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 8: Synchronize sequences\\\\n\\\\nAfter initial data sync is complete, but BEFORE switching to Supabase:\\\\n\\\\n```bash\\\\n# Set source to read-only\\\\npsql -h <source_host> -c \\\\\\\"ALTER DATABASE <source_database> SET default_transaction_read_only = true;\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\n# Export sequences from source\\\\npg_dump \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -h <source_host> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -U <source_user> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -p <source_port> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  -d <source_database> \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --data-only \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --table='*_seq' \\\\\\\\\\\\n  --table='*_id_seq' > sequences.sql\\\\n\\\\n# Import sequences to Supabase\\\\npsql \\\\\\\"$SUPABASE_DB_URL\\\\\\\" -f sequences.sql\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 9: Switch to Supabase\\\\n\\\\n1.  Ensure replication lag is zero:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- On Supabase\\\\nselect * from pg_stat_subscription;\\\\n-- Check that latest_end_lsn is current\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n2.  Stop writes to the source database (if not already read-only)\\\\n\\\\n3.  Drop subscription on Supabase:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nDROP SUBSCRIPTION supabase_subscription;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n4.  Update application connection strings to point to Supabase\\\\n\\\\n5.  Verify application functionality\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Step 10: Cleanup\\\\n\\\\nOn source database (after successful migration):\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\n-- Remove publication\\\\nDROP PUBLICATION supabase_migration;\\\\n\\\\n-- Check and remove any remaining replication slots\\\\nSELECT * FROM pg_replication_slots;\\\\nDROP REPLICATION SLOT slot_name;  -- if any remain\\\\n\\\\n-- The source database should remain read-only or be decommissioned\\\\n-- Do NOT re-enable writes to avoid a split-brain scenario!\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Troubleshooting logical replication\\\\n\\\\n| Issue                                | Solution                                                            |\\\\n| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\\\n| \\\\\\\"could not connect to the publisher\\\\\\\" | Check network connectivity, firewall rules, pg\\\\\\\\_hba.conf            |\\\\n| \\\\\\\"role does not exist\\\\\\\"                | Ensure replication user exists on source with REPLICATION privilege |\\\\n| \\\\\\\"publication does not exist\\\\\\\"         | Verify publication name and that it was created successfully        |\\\\n| Replication lag growing              | Check network bandwidth, source database load, add more WAL senders |\\\\n| Tables stuck in `i` state            | Check for locks on source tables, verify table structure matches    |\\\\n| \\\\\\\"out of replication slots\\\\\\\"           | Increase max\\\\\\\\_replication\\\\\\\\_slots in Postgres.conf                   |\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Important limitations\\\\n\\\\n*   **DDL changes**: Schema modifications are not replicated - freeze schema during migration\\\\n*   **Sequences**: Need manual synchronization before cutover\\\\n*   **Large Objects (LOBs)**: Not replicated - use dump/restore or store in regular bytea columns\\\\n*   **Custom types**: May need special handling\\\\n*   **Users and roles**: Must be recreated manually on Supabase\\\\n\\\\nFor detailed restrictions, see [Postgres Logical Replication Restrictions](https://www.Postgres.org/docs/current/logical-replication-restrictions.html)\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### When to use which method\\\\n\\\\n**Use Dump/Restore when:**\\\\n\\\\n*   Downtime window is acceptable\\\\n*   Source is Postgres \\\\\\\\< 10\\\\n*   Simpler process preferred\\\\n*   Cannot configure logical replication on the source\\\\n\\\\n**Use Logical Replication when:**\\\\n\\\\n*   Minimal downtime required\\\\n*   Postgres 10+ on both sides\\\\n*   Can modify source configuration\\\\n*   Have replication privileges\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Getting help\\\\n\\\\n*   For databases > 150 GB: [Contact Supabase support](/dashboard/support/new) before starting\\\\n*   [Supabase Dashboard Support](/dashboard/support/new)\\\\n*   [Supabase Discord](https://discord.supabase.com)\\\\n* migration\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Postgres Roles\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/roles\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Postgres Roles\\\\n\\\\nManaging access to your Postgres database and configuring permissions.\\\\n\\\\nPostgres manages database access permissions using the concept of roles. Generally you wouldn't use these roles for your own application - they are mostly for configuring *system access* to your database. If you want to configure *application access*, then you should use [Row Level Security](/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security) (RLS). You can also implement [Role-based Access Control](/docs/guides/database/postgres/custom-claims-and-role-based-access-control-rbac) on top of RLS.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Users vs roles\\\\n\\\\nIn Postgres, roles can function as users or groups of users. Users are roles with login privileges, while groups (also known as role groups) are roles that don't have login privileges but can be used to manage permissions for multiple users.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Creating roles\\\\n\\\\nYou can create a role using the `create role` command:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate role \\\\\\\"role_name\\\\\\\";\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Creating users\\\\n\\\\nRoles and users are essentially the same in Postgres, however if you want to use password-logins for a specific role, then you can use `WITH LOGIN PASSWORD`:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate role \\\\\\\"role_name\\\\\\\" with login password 'extremely_secure_password';\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Passwords\\\\n\\\\nYour Postgres database is the core of your Supabase project, so it's important that every role has a strong, secure password at all times. Here are some tips for creating a secure password:\\\\n\\\\n*   Use a password manager to generate it.\\\\n*   Make a long password (12 characters at least).\\\\n*   Don't use any common dictionary words.\\\\n*   Use both upper and lower case characters, numbers, and special symbols.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Special symbols in passwords\\\\n\\\\nIf you use special symbols in your Postgres password, you must remember to [percent-encode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent-encoding) your password later if using the Postgres connection string, for example, `postgresql://postgres.projectref:p%3Dword@aws-0-us-east-1.pooler.supabase.com:6543/postgres`\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Changing your project password\\\\n\\\\nWhen you created your project you were also asked to enter a password. This is the password for the `postgres` role in your database. You can update this from the Dashboard under the [Database Settings](/dashboard/project/_/database/settings) page. You should *never* give this to third-party service unless you absolutely trust them. Instead, we recommend that you create a new user for every service that you want to give access too. This will also help you with debugging - you can see every query that each role is executing in your database within `pg_stat_statements`.\\\\n\\\\nChanging the password does not result in any downtime. All connected services, such as PostgREST, PgBouncer, and other Supabase managed services, are automatically updated to use the latest password to ensure availability. However, if you have any external services connecting to the Supabase database using hardcoded username/password credentials, a manual update will be required.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Granting permissions\\\\n\\\\nRoles can be granted various permissions on database objects using the `GRANT` command. Permissions include `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE`. You can configure access to almost any object inside your database - including tables, views, functions, and triggers.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Revoking permissions\\\\n\\\\nPermissions can be revoked using the `REVOKE` command:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nREVOKE permission_type ON object_name FROM role_name;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Role hierarchy\\\\n\\\\nRoles can be organized in a hierarchy, where one role can inherit permissions from another. This simplifies permission management, as you can define permissions at a higher level and have them automatically apply to all child roles.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Role inheritance\\\\n\\\\nTo create a role hierarchy, you first need to create the parent and child roles. The child role will inherit permissions from its parent. Child roles can be added using the INHERIT option when creating the role:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\ncreate role \\\\\\\"child_role_name\\\\\\\" inherit \\\\\\\"parent_role_name\\\\\\\";\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### Preventing inheritance\\\\n\\\\nIn some cases, you might want to prevent a role from having a child relationship (typically superuser roles). You can prevent inheritance relations using `NOINHERIT`:\\\\n\\\\n```sql\\\\nalter role \\\\\\\"child_role_name\\\\\\\" noinherit;\\\\n```\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Supabase roles\\\\n\\\\nPostgres comes with a set of [predefined roles](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/predefined-roles.html). Supabase extends this with a default set of roles which are configured on your database when you start a new project:\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `postgres`\\\\n\\\\nThe default Postgres role. This has admin privileges.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `anon`\\\\n\\\\nFor unauthenticated, public access. This is the role which the API (PostgREST) will use when a user *is not* logged in.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `authenticator`\\\\n\\\\nA special role for the API (PostgREST). It has very limited access, and is used to validate a JWT and then\\\\n\\\\\\\"change into\\\\\\\" another role determined by the JWT verification.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `authenticated`\\\\n\\\\nFor \\\\\\\"authenticated access.\\\\\\\" This is the role which the API (PostgREST) will use when a user *is* logged in.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `service_role`\\\\n\\\\nFor elevated access. This role is used by the API (PostgREST) to bypass Row Level Security.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `supabase_auth_admin`\\\\n\\\\nUsed by the Auth middleware to connect to the database and run migration. Access is scoped to the `auth` schema.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `supabase_storage_admin`\\\\n\\\\nUsed by the Auth middleware to connect to the database and run migration. Access is scoped to the `storage` schema.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `supabase_etl_admin`\\\\n\\\\nUsed by [Replication powered by Supabase ETL](/docs/guides/database/replication) to replicate database changes to external destinations. Has read-all access and replication privileges for change data capture, bypasses Row Level Security, and can write to the `etl` schema.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `dashboard_user`\\\\n\\\\nFor running commands via the Supabase UI.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n### `supabase_admin`\\\\n\\\\nAn internal role Supabase uses for administrative tasks, such as running upgrades and automations.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Resources\\\\n\\\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Database Roles](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/database-roles.html)\\\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Role Membership](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/role-membership.html)\\\\n*   Official Postgres docs: [Function Permissions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/perm-functions.html)\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Branching via the dashboard\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/deployment/branching/dashboard\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Branching via the dashboard\\\\n\\\\nCreate, manage, review, and merge branches directly in the dashboard\\\\n\\\\nYou can create, manage, review, and merge Supabase branches directly via the dashboard. This is useful for quick testing, prototyping, or when you prefer to work in a no-code way. You can also connect a Supabase branch to a GitHub branch at a later time if needed.\\\\n\\\\n<Admonition type=\\\\\\\"note\\\\\\\" label=\\\\\\\"Public Alpha\\\\\\\">\\\\n  Branch management via the dashboard is currently in public alpha. Features and functionality may change.\\\\n</Admonition>\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## How Branching works\\\\n\\\\nYou can do the following directly from the Supabase dashboard:\\\\n\\\\n*   Create preview branches\\\\n*   Make changes to your public schema or edge functions\\\\n*   Merge these changes back into production when ready\\\\n*   Pull in updates from production\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Enable branch management via the dashboard\\\\n\\\\nThis functionality is currently in beta and requires opting in. To opt in you must enable the feature preview:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Open the user menu by clicking on your user icon in the top right.\\\\n2.  Select **Branching via dashboard**.\\\\n3.  Click **Enable feature**.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Creating a branch\\\\n\\\\nOnce you've enabled the feature, you can create a new branch:\\\\n\\\\n1.  Click the arrows next to the branch name in the top menu bar. (The top menu bar has the format `YOUR_ORGANIZATION / YOUR_PROJECT / CURRENT_BRANCH_NAME`.)\\\\n2.  Click `Create branch`.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Making changes to a branch\\\\n\\\\nUse the branch selector in the top bar to change to your branch. Any changes you make (including SQL run in the SQL editor, table editor changes, and configuration changes) are now made against the currently selected branch.\\\\n\\\\nYou can also use the branch's API keys and connection strings to run changes against the branch from your own code or SQL client.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Creating a merge request\\\\n\\\\nTo review and merge changes from a branch back into your production branch, you must first create a merge request. There are two ways to do this.\\\\n\\\\nThe first is to click the merge request button next to the branch selector that's located in the top menu. This will create the merge request and redirect you to the merge page where you can review and merge any changes.\\\\n\\\\nThe second is to click on manage branches from within the branch selector, then in the left hand navigation you can click on merge requests. From here you can view all open merge requests and create new ones.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Pulling changes from production into a branch\\\\n\\\\nWhen reviewing a merge request you may see a notice at the top of the page asking you to update your branch. This appears when your preview branch has drifted from your production branch. There may be public schema or edge function changes that have been made after your preview branch was created. Clicking update branch will attempt to pull in these changes, but be aware that by doing this your existing edge functions will be replaced. Any new edge functions created on the preview branch will remain untouched.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Limitations\\\\n\\\\nThere are a few limitations you should be aware of before deciding to use branching without git.\\\\n\\\\n*   Custom roles created through the dashboard are not captured on branch creation\\\\n*   Branches can only be merged to main; merging between preview branches is not supported\\\\n*   If your branch is out of date, you can pull in latest changes from main, but keep in mind that all functions will be overwritten\\\\n*   Deleting functions must be done manually on main branch\\\\n*   Migration conflicts must be manually resolved on the preview branch\\\\n*   If you have run migrations on main, new branches will be created from existing migrations instead of a full schema dump\\\\n\\\"},{\\\"title\\\":\\\"Working with branches\\\",\\\"href\\\":\\\"https://supabase.com/docs/guides/deployment/branching/working-with-branches\\\",\\\"content\\\":\\\"# Working with branches\\\\n\\\\nLearn how to develop and manage your Supabase branches\\\\n\\\\nThis guide covers how to work with Supabase branches effectively, including migration management, seeding behavior, and development workflows.\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n## Subscribing to notifications\\\\n\\\\nYou can subscribe to webhook notifications when an action run completes on a persistent branch.
